titleStmt.title: POSTER ABSTRACT: Preemptive Uniprocessor EDF Schedulability Analysis with Preemption Costs Considered

div.p: We are exploring preemption-costs cognizant schedulability and sustainability issues in the uniprocessor EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems. Let us take a closer look at a preemption operation:

div.head: A preempting (checked lines) and preempted (horizontal lines) job with context switch costs (solid black).
div.p: The figure above depicts (with horizontal lines) an executing job with deadline at t f , that is preempted at time-instant t 1 , by a newly-arrived job (in checked lines) with an earlier deadline. The durations devoted to context-switch operations are depicted as solid black boxes; there is one such duration when the job is preempted (the "context-switch save" cost), and another when the preempted job is resumed (the "contextswitch restore" cost). We enhance the standard three-parameter sporadic task model by associating with each sporadic task τ i the parameters css i and csr i in addition to the "standard" WCET (C i ), relative deadline (D i ), and period (T i ) parameters. Here, css i denotes the maximum duration needed to save the context associated with an executing job of τ i that is preempted, while csr i denotes the maximum duration of time needed to restore this context when the job is resumed.

Observation 1. Any preemption operation requires that two sub-operations be performed: (i) a context-switch save operation when preemption occurs, and (ii) a context-switch restore operation when the preempted job later resumes.
1) The save operation occurs before the preempting job's execution and preempting job's deadline.
2) The restore operation need not complete prior to the deadline of the preempting job.
3) The preempting job may not always be the one that restores the context.

div.head: The third observation above is illustrated in the following figure:
div.p: A job (diagonal lines) with deadline between those of the preempting and preempted jobs arrives at time-instant t 2 .

Sustainability [1, page 159]. For EDF scheduling, we have established that (i) scheduling of sporadic task systems is sustainable with respect to WCET parameters and context switch costs; and (ii) scheduling of implicit-deadline sporadic task systems is not sustainable with respect to period parameters even if all context-switch costs are equal.

Schedulability analysis. We have developed a "safe" transformation from the problem of EDF-schedulability analysis when preemption durations are non-zero to the problem of EDF-schedulability analysis when preemption durations are all equal to zero:
div.formula: Theorem 1. A sporadic task system τ = τ i = (C i , D i , T i , css i , csr i ) n i=1 is EDF-schedulable if the sporadic task system τ = (C i , D i , T i , 0, 0) n i=1 is EDF-schedulable,
div.p: with the C i 's defined as follows:
div.formula: C i ← C i + max Dj >Di {css j + csr j }
div.p: Ongoing Work. We are currently working on reducing the pessimism in Theorem 1. We are also exploring computational complexity issues -although it is straightforward to show that preemption-cognizant analysis is NP-hard for sporadic task systems in general, we do not yet know whether such analysis is intractable or not for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems.
